claims.text: The as-synthesized nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst has a homogeneous distribution of metal atoms.
Controlled thermal annealing can reorder the atomic configuration of PtPdRhRuIrOs without causing phase segregation.
Annealing-induced atomic reordering shifts the Pt d-band center.
The shifted Pt d-band center results from enhanced p–d orbital hybridization with neighboring alloying atoms.
The altered electronic structure of Pt sites reduces the adsorption energy of strongly binding carbonaceous poisoning intermediates during ethanol oxidation.
Reduced poisoning-intermediate adsorption favors a less-poisoning ethanol-oxidation pathway.
Reducing catalyst poisoning enhances ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
Reducing catalyst poisoning enhances catalyst durability.
Annealed PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts will have lower coverage of poisoning species than unannealed catalysts.
Annealed catalysts will produce a higher fraction of desired ethanol-oxidation products such as acetaldehyde or acetic acid.
Annealed catalysts will exhibit improved durability during electrochemical cycling.
The predicted behavior holds under moderate annealing conditions that preserve the single-phase solid solution.
The predicted behavior holds within the potential window typical of ethanol oxidation.
Excessive annealing that causes phase segregation may eliminate the predicted improvements.
Electronic-structure tuning through p–d orbital hybridization has been observed in a Pt-based high-entropy-alloy catalyst for methanol oxidation.
In the cited PtRuNiCoFeGaPbW catalyst, p–d hybridization and optimized electronic structure suppress CO-intermediate formation or adsorption and favor a non-CO methanol-oxidation pathway.
Unannealed PtPdRhRuIrOs tested under otherwise identical ethanol-oxidation conditions is the experimental baseline.
Failure of annealing to produce statistically significant reductions in poisoning adsorption, improved product selectivity, or improved durability would falsify the proposed mechanism.
